Quantum Wasserstein distance based on an optimization over separable states

Géza Tóth Email: toth@alumni.nd.edu Affiliation: Theoretical Physics, University of the Basque Country UPV/EHU, ES-48080 Bilbao, Spain Affiliation: EHU Quantum Center, University of the Basque Country UPV/EHU, Barrio Sarriena s/n, ES-48940 Leioa, Biscay, Spain Affiliation: Donostia International Physics Center (DIPC), ES-20080 San Sebastián, Spain Affiliation: IKERBASQUE, Basque Foundation for Science, ES-48011 Bilbao, Spain Affiliation: Institute for Solid State Physics and Optics, Wigner Research Centre for Physics, HU-1525 Budapest, Hungary    József Pitrik Email: pitrik@math.bme.hu Affiliation: Institute for Solid State Physics and Optics, Wigner Research Centre for Physics, HU-1525 Budapest, Hungary Affiliation: Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics, Reáltanoda u. 13-15., HU-1053 Budapest, Hungary Affiliation: Department of Analysis and Operations Research, Institute of Mathematics, Budapest University of Technology and Economics, Műegyetem rkp. 3., HU-1111 Budapest, Hungary
Abstract

We define the quantum Wasserstein distance such that the optimization of the coupling is carried out over bipartite separable states rather than bipartite quantum states in general, and examine its properties. Surprisingly, we find that the self-distance is related to the quantum Fisher information. We present a transport map corresponding to an optimal bipartite separable state. We discuss how the quantum Wasserstein distance introduced is connected to criteria detecting quantum entanglement. We define variance-like quantities that can be obtained from the quantum Wasserstein distance by replacing the minimization over quantum states by a maximization. We extend our results to a family of generalized quantum Fisher information quantities.

Dedicated to the memory of Dénes Petz on the occasion of his 70th birthday.

1 Introduction

A classical Wasserstein distance is a metric between probability distributions μ\mu and ν,\nu, induced by the problem of optimal mass transportation [1, 2]. It reflects the minimal effort that is required in order to morph the mass of μ\mu into the mass distribution of ν\nu. Methods based on the theory of optimal transport and advantageous properties of Wasserstein metrics have achieved great success in several important fields of pure mathematics including probability theory [3, 4], theory of (stochastic) partial differential equations [5, 6], variational problems [7, 8] and geometry of metric spaces [9, 10, 11, 12]. In recent years, there have been a lot of results concerning the description of isometries of Wasserstein spaces, too [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. Moreover, optimal transport and Wasserstein metric are also used as tools in applied mathematics. In particular, there are applications to image and signal processing [20, 21, 22], medical imaging [23, 24] and machine learning [25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30].

The non-commutative generalization, the so-called quantum optimal transport has been at the center of attention, as it lead to the definition of several new and very useful notions in quantum physics. The first, semi-classical approach of Życzkowski and Slomczynski, has been motivated by applications in quantum chaos [31, 32, 33]. The method of Biane and Voiculescu is related to free probability [34], while the one of Carlen, Maas, Datta, and Rouzé [35, 36, 37, 38, 39] is based on a dynamical interpretation. Caglioti, Golse, Mouhot, and Paul presented an approach based on a static interpretation [40, 41, 42, 43, 44, 45]. Finally De Palma and Trevisan used quantum channels [46], and De Palma, Marvian, Trevisan, and Lloyd defined the quantum earth mover’s distance, i.e., the quantum Wasserstein distance order 1 [47], while Bistron, Cole, Eckstein, Friedland and Życzkowski formulated a quantum Wasserstein distance based on an antisymmetric cost function [48, 49, 50].

One of the key results of quantum optimal transport is the definition of the quantum Wasserstein distance [31, 32, 33, 40, 41, 42, 43, 46, 47, 44, 45, 51, 52]. It has the often desirable feature that it is not necessarily maximal for two quantum states orthogonal to each other, which is beneficial, for instance, when performing learning on quantum data [53]. Some of the properties of the new quantities are puzzling, yet point to profound relations between seemingly unrelated fields of quantum physics. For instance, the quantum Wasserstein distance order 2 of the quantum state from itself can be nonzero, while in the classical case the self-distance is always zero. In particular, as we have mentioned, the quantum Wasserstein distance has been defined based on a quantum channel formalism [46], and it has been shown that the square of the self-distance is equal to the Wigner-Yanase skew information of the quantum state [54]. At this point the questions arises: Can other fields of quantum physics help to interpret these results? For example, is it possible to relate the findings above to entanglement theory [55, 56, 57] such that we obtain new and meaningful relations naturally?

Before presenting our results, let us summarize the definitions of the quantum Wasserstein distance.

Definition 1. The square of the distance between two quantum states described by the density matrices ϱ\varrho and σ\sigma is given by De Palma and Trevisan as [46]

DDPT(ϱ,σ)2=12minϱ12∑n=1N\displaystyle D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\min_{\varrho_{12}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\; Tr⁡[(HnT⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Hn)2​ϱ12],\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[(H_{n}^{T}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H_{n})^{2}\varrho_{12}],
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒟,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{D},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱT,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho^{T},
Tr1​(ϱ12)=σ,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\sigma, (1)

where ATA^{T} denotes the matrix transpose of A,A, and H1,H2,…,HNH_{1},H_{2},...,H_{N} are Hermitian operators 11 1 We use the convention that in the expression within the trace in Eq. (1), Hn⊗𝟙H_{n}\otimes\mathbbm{1} denotes an operator in which HnH_{n} acts on subsystem 11 and 𝟙\mathbbm{1} acts on subsystem 2.2., while 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the set of density matrices, i.e., Hermitian matrices fulfilling

ϱ12=ϱ12†,Tr⁡(ϱ12)=1,ϱ12≥0.\varrho_{12}=\varrho_{12}^{\dagger},{\rm Tr}(\varrho_{12})=1,\varrho_{12}\geq 0. (2)

In this approach, there is a bipartite density matrix ϱ12,\varrho_{12}, called coupling, corresponding to any transport map between ϱ\varrho and σ,\sigma, and vice versa, there is a transport map corresponding to any coupling [46]. Moreover, it has been shown that for the self-distance of a state [46]

DDPT​(ϱ,ϱ)2=∑n=1NIϱ​(Hn)D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\varrho)^{2}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}I_{\varrho}(H_{n}) (3)

holds, where the Wigner-Yanase skew information is defined as [54]

Iϱ​(H)=Tr⁡(H2​ϱ)−Tr⁡(H​ϱ​H​ϱ).I_{\varrho}(H)={\rm Tr}(H^{2}\varrho)-{\rm Tr}(H\sqrt{\varrho}H\sqrt{\varrho}). (4)

This profound result connects seemingly two very different notions of quantum physics, as it has been mentioned in the introduction.

The Wasserstein distance has also been defined in a slightly different way.

Definition 2. Golse, Mouhot, Paul and Caglioti defined the square of the distance as [40, 45, 43, 41, 42, 44]

DGMPC​(ϱ,σ)2\displaystyle D_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\quad\quad\quad
=12minϱ12∑n=1N\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\min_{\varrho_{12}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\; Tr⁡[(Hn⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Hn)2​ϱ12],\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[(H_{n}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H_{n})^{2}\varrho_{12}],
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒟,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{D},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱ,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho,
Tr1​(ϱ12)=σ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\sigma. (5)

In this paper, we will obtain new quantities by restricting the optimization to separable states in the above definitions. We will show that, in this case, the square of the self-distance equals the quantum Fisher information times a constant, while in Eq. (3) it was related to the Wigner-Yanase skew information. The quantum Fisher information is a central quantity in quantum estimation theory and quantum metrology, a field that is concerned with metrological tasks in which the quantumness of the system plays an essential role [58, 59, 60, 61]. Recent findings show that the quantum Fisher information is the convex roof of the variance, apart from a constant factor [62, 63], which allowed, for instance, to derive novel uncertainty relations [64, 65], and will also be used in this article.

The paper is organized as follows. In Sec. 2, we summarize basic facts connected to quantum metrology. In Sec. 3, we summarize entanglement theory. In Sec. 4, we show how to transform the optimization over decompositions of the density matrix into an optimization of an expectation value over separable states. In Sec. 5, we show some applications of these ideas for the Wasserstein distance. We define a novel type of Wasserstein distance based on an optimization over separable states. In Sec. 6, we define variance-like quantities from the Wasserstein distance. In Sec. 7, we discuss how such a Wasserstein distance and the variance-like quantity mentioned above can be used to construct entanglement criteria. In Sec. 8, we introduce further quantities similar to the formulas giving the Wasserstein distance, but they involve the variance of two-body quantities rather than the second moment. In Sec. 9, we consider an optimization over various subsets of the quantum states. In Sec. 10, we extend our ideas to various generalized quantum Fisher information quanitities.

2 Quantum metrology

Before discussing our main results, we review some of the fundamental relations of quantum metrology. A basic metrological task is estimating the small angle θ\theta in a unitary dynamics

Uθ=exp⁡(−i​H​θ),U_{\theta}=\exp(-i{H}\theta), (6)

where HH is the Hamiltonian. The precision is limited by the Cramér-Rao bound as [66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 58, 60, 61, 71, 72, 59, 73]

(Δ​θ)2≥1ν​ℱQ​[ϱ,H],(\Delta\theta)^{2}\geq\frac{1}{\nu{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,{H}]}, (7)

where the factor 1/ν1/\nu in Eq. (7) is the statistical improvement when performing independent measurements on identical copies of the probe state, and the quantum Fisher information is defined by the formula [66, 67, 68, 69, 70]

ℱQ​[ϱ,H]=2​∑k,l(λk−λl)2λk+λl​|⟨k|H|l⟩|2,{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,{H}]=2\sum_{k,l}\frac{(\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{l})^{2}}{\lambda_{k}+\lambda_{l}}|\langle k|{H}|l\rangle|^{2}, (8)

where the density matrix has the eigendecomposition

ϱ=∑kλk​|k⟩​⟨k|.\varrho=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}|k\rangle\langle k|. (9)

The quantum Fisher information is bounded from above by the variance and from below by the Wigner-Yanase skew information as

4​Iϱ​(H)≤ℱQ​[ϱ,H]≤4​(Δ​H)ϱ2,4I_{\varrho}(H)\leq{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H]\leq 4(\Delta H)^{2}_{\varrho}, (10)

where if ϱ\varrho is pure then the equality holds for both inequalities [68]. For clarity, we add that the variance is defined as

(Δ​H)ϱ2=⟨H2⟩ϱ−⟨H⟩ϱ2,(\Delta H)^{2}_{\varrho}=\langle{H^{2}}\rangle_{\varrho}-\langle{H}\rangle^{2}_{\varrho}, (11)

where the expectation value is calculated as

⟨H⟩ϱ=Tr⁡(ϱ​H).\langle{H}\rangle_{\varrho}={\rm Tr}(\varrho H). (12)

The quantum Fisher information is the convex roof of the variance times four [62, 63, 71]

ℱQ​[ϱ,H]=4​min⁡∑k{pk,|Ψk⟩}⁡pk​(Δ​H)Ψk2,{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H]=4\min_{\{p_{k},|\Psi_{k}\rangle\}}\;\sum_{k}p_{k}(\Delta H)^{2}_{\Psi_{k}}, (13)

where the optimization is carried out over pure state decompositions of the type

ϱ=∑kpk​|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|.\varrho=\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|. (14)

For the probabilities pk≥0p_{k}\geq 0 and ∑kpk=1\sum_{k}p_{k}=1 hold, and the pure states |Ψk⟩|\Psi_{k}\rangle are not assumed to be orthogonal to each other.

Apart from the quantum Fisher information, the variance can also be given as a roof [62, 63]

(Δ​H)ϱ2=max⁡∑k{pk,|Ψk⟩}⁡pk​(Δ​H)Ψk2.(\Delta H)^{2}_{\varrho}=\max_{\{p_{k},|\Psi_{k}\rangle\}}\;\sum_{k}p_{k}(\Delta H)^{2}_{\Psi_{k}}. (15)

Note that convex and concave roofs of more complicated expressions can also be computed. For instance,

min⁡∑k{pk,|Ψk⟩}⁡pk​∑n=1N(Δ​Hn)Ψk2≥14​∑n=1NℱQ​[ϱ,Hn],\min_{\{p_{k},|\Psi_{k}\rangle\}}\sum_{k}p_{k}\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\Psi_{k}}\geq\frac{1}{4}\sum_{n=1}^{N}{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H_{n}], (16)

and the expression

max⁡∑k{pk,|Ψk⟩}⁡pk​∑n=1N(Δ​Hn)Ψk2≤∑n=1N(Δ​Hn)ϱ2,\max_{\{p_{k},|\Psi_{k}\rangle\}}\sum_{k}p_{k}\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\Psi_{k}}\leq\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\varrho}, (17)

are the convex and concave roofs, respectively, of the sum of several variances over the decompositions of ϱ\varrho given in Eq. (14). They play a role in the derivation of entanglement conditions [64], and will also appear in our results about the quantum Wasserstein distance. We add that there is an equality in Eq. (17) for N=2N=2 [74, 75].

Finally, we note that the quantum Fisher information can also be given with a minimization over purifications, which has been used, for instance, to study quantum metrology in noisy systems [76, 77, 78]. The relation of this finding to the expression in Eq. (13) is discussed in Ref. [79].

3 Entanglement theory

Next, we review entanglement theory [55, 56, 57]. A bipartite quantum state is separable if it can be given as [80]

∑kpk​|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|⊗|Φk⟩​⟨Φk|,\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|\otimes|\Phi_{k}\rangle\langle\Phi_{k}|, (18)

where pkp_{k} are for the probabilities, |Ψk⟩|\Psi_{k}\rangle and |Φk⟩|\Phi_{k}\rangle are pure quantum states. We will denote the set of separable states by 𝒮.\mathcal{S}. The mixture of two separable states is also separable, thus the set 𝒮\mathcal{S} is convex. If a quantum state cannot be written as Eq. (18) then it is called entangled.

A relevant subset of separable states are the symmetric separable states, which can be given as [81, 82]

∑kpk​|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|⊗|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|.\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|\otimes|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|. (19)

We will denote the set of symmetric separable states by 𝒮′.\mathcal{S}^{\prime}. The mixture of two symmetric separable states is also symmetric and separable, thus the set S′S^{\prime} is also convex. Clearly

𝒮′⊂𝒮.\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{S}. (20)

For such states for the expectation value

⟨Ps⟩=1\langle{P_{s}}\rangle=1 (21)

holds, where PsP_{s} is the projector to the symmetric subspace defined by the basis vectors |n​n⟩|nn\rangle and (|n​m⟩+|m​n⟩)/2(|nm\rangle+|mn\rangle)/\sqrt{2} for n≠m.n\neq m. Equivalently, any state in S′S^{\prime} fulfills

F12​ϱ=ϱ​F12=ϱ,F_{12}\varrho=\varrho F_{12}=\varrho, (22)

where F12F_{12} is the flip operator for which

F12​|m⟩⊗|n⟩=|n⟩⊗|m⟩F_{12}|m\rangle\otimes|n\rangle=|n\rangle\otimes|m\rangle (23)

for all m,n.m,n.

The set of quantum states with a positive partial transpose (PPT) 𝒫\mathcal{P} consists of the states for which

ϱTk≥0\varrho^{T_{k}}\geq 0 (24)

holds for k=1,2,k=1,2, where TkT_{k} is a partial transposition according to the kt​hk^{th} subsystem. 𝒫\mathcal{P} is clearly a convex set. Moreover, all separable states given in Eq. (18) fulfill Eq. (24), thus

𝒫⊃𝒮\mathcal{P}\supset\mathcal{S} (25)

holds. For two qubits and for a qubit-qutrit system, i.e., for 2×22\times 2 and 2×32\times 3 systems the set of PPT states equals the set of separable states [83, 84, 85].

It is generally very difficult to decide whether a state is separable or not, while it is very simple to decide whether the condition given in Eq. (24) is fulfilled. Such conditions can be even part of semidefinite programs used to solve various optimization problems (e.g., Ref. [86]). Thus, often the set of PPT quantum states, 𝒫\mathcal{P} is used instead of the separable states. Since for small systems 𝒫=𝒮,\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{S}, optimization problems over separable states can be solved exactly for those cases. For larger systems, by optimizing over states in 𝒫\mathcal{P} instead of states in 𝒮,\mathcal{S}, we get lower or upper bounds.

Finally, we will define the set of symmetric PPT states 𝒫′.\mathcal{P}^{\prime}. States in this set are symmetric, thus Eqs. (21) and (22) hold. For the various sets mentioned above, we have the relation

𝒮′⊂𝒫′⊂𝒫,\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{P}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{P}, (26)

while for 2×22\times 2 and 2×32\times 3 systems, we have P′=S′.P^{\prime}=S^{\prime}.

Convex roofs and concave roofs play also a central role in entanglement theory. The entanglement of formation is defined as a convex roof over pure components of the von Neumann entropy of the reduced state [87, 88]

EF​(ϱ)=min⁡∑k{pk,|Ψk⟩}⁡pk​EE​(Ψk),E_{F}(\varrho)=\min_{\{p_{k},|\Psi_{k}\rangle\}}\sum_{k}p_{k}E_{E}(\Psi_{k}), (27)

where the optimization is over the decompositions given in Eq. (14), and the entanglement entropy of the pure components is given as

EE​(Ψk)=S⁡[TrA​(Ψk)],E_{E}(\Psi_{k})=S[{\rm Tr}_{A}(\Psi_{k})], (28)

where SS is the von Neumann entropy. EF​(ϱ)E_{F}(\varrho) is the minimum entanglement needed to create the state. On the other hand, the entanglement of assistance is obtained as a concave roof [89, 90]

EA​(ϱ)=max⁡∑k{pk,|Ψk⟩}⁡pk​EE​(Ψk).E_{A}(\varrho)=\max_{\{p_{k},|\Psi_{k}\rangle\}}\;\sum_{k}p_{k}E_{E}(\Psi_{k}). (29)

The above quantities correspond to the following scenario. Let us assume that the bipartite quantum state ϱ\varrho living on parties AA and BB is realized as the reduced state of a pure state living on parties A,BA,B and C.C. Let us assume that party CC makes a von Neumann measurement resulting in a state |Ψk⟩|\Psi_{k}\rangle on AA and B,B, and it sends the measurement result kk to AA and B.B. After repeating this on many copies of the three-partite state, the average entanglement of AA and BB will be

∑kpk​EE​(Ψk),\sum_{k}p_{k}E_{E}(\Psi_{k}), (30)

where pkp_{k} is the probability of the outcome kk and and for the |Ψk⟩|\Psi_{k}\rangle states Eq. (14) holds. If party C wants to help the parties AA and BB to have a large average entanglement, then Eq. (30) can reach the entanglement of assistance given in Eq. (29). On the other hand, the average entanglement is always larger than or equal to the entanglement of formation given in Eq. (27).

Next, we will introduce an entanglement condition based on the sum of several variances [91, 92, 93, 94], which will be used later in the article. Let us consider a full set of traceless observables {Gn}n=1d2−1\{G_{n}\}_{n=1}^{d^{2}-1} for dd-dimensional systems fulfilling

Tr⁡(Gn​Gn′)=2​δn​n′.{\rm Tr}(G_{n}G_{n^{\prime}})=2\delta_{nn^{\prime}}. (31)

Any traceless Hermitian observable can be obtained as a linear combination of Gn.G_{n}. In other words, GnG_{n} are the SU(dd) generators. It is known that for pure states (see e.g., Ref. [94])

∑n=1d2−1(Δ​Gn)2=2​(d−1)\sum_{n=1}^{d^{2}-1}(\Delta G_{n})^{2}=2(d-1) (32)

holds. Due to the concavity of the variance it follows that for mixed states we have [94]

∑n=1d2−1(Δ​Gn)2≥2​(d−1).\sum_{n=1}^{d^{2}-1}(\Delta G_{n})^{2}\geq 2(d-1). (33)

Let us now consider a d×dd\times d system. For a product state, |Ψ⟩⊗|Φ⟩,|\Psi\rangle\otimes|\Phi\rangle, we obtain [91, 94]

∑n=1d2−1[Δ⁡(GnT⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Gn)]Ψ⊗Φ2\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{d^{2}-1}[\Delta(G_{n}^{T}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes G_{n})]^{2}_{\Psi\otimes\Phi}
=∑n=1d2−1(Δ​GnT)Ψ2+∑n=1d2−1(Δ​Gn)Φ2\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad=\sum_{n=1}^{d^{2}-1}(\Delta G_{n}^{T})^{2}_{\Psi}+\sum_{n=1}^{d^{2}-1}(\Delta G_{n})^{2}_{\Phi}
=4​(d−1),\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad=4(d-1), (34)

where in the last inequality we used that for pure states Eq. (32) holds. We also used the fact that if {Gn}n=1d2−1\{G_{n}\}_{n=1}^{d^{2}-1} is a full set of observables with the properties mentioned above, then {GnT}n=1d2−1\{G_{n}^{T}\}_{n=1}^{d^{2}-1} is also a full set of such observables. Then, for bipartite separable states given in Eq. (18) [91, 92, 93, 94]

∑n=1d2−1[Δ⁡(GnT⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Gn)]2≥4​(d−1)\sum_{n=1}^{d^{2}-1}[\Delta(G_{n}^{T}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes G_{n})]^{2}\geq 4(d-1) (35)

holds due to the concavity of the variance. Any state that violates the inequality in Eq. (35) is entangled. The left-hand side of Eq. (35) is zero for the maximally entangled state

|Ψme⟩=1d​∑k=0d−1|k⟩​|k⟩.|\Psi_{\rm me}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}|k\rangle|k\rangle. (36)

Thus, we say that the criterion given in Eq. (35) detects entangled states in the vicinity of the state given in Eq. (36).

Let us consider the d=2d=2 case concretely. Let us choose {Gn}n=13={σx,σy,σz}.\{G_{n}\}_{n=1}^{3}=\{\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y},\sigma_{z}\}. Equation (35) can rewritten as

[Δ⁡(σx⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗σx)]2\displaystyle[\Delta(\sigma_{x}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes\sigma_{x})]^{2}
+[Δ⁡(σy⊗𝟙+𝟙⊗σy)]2\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad+[\Delta(\sigma_{y}\otimes\mathbbm{1}+\mathbbm{1}\otimes\sigma_{y})]^{2}
+[Δ⁡(σz⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗σz)]2≥4,\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad+[\Delta(\sigma_{z}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes\sigma_{z})]^{2}\geq 4, (37)

where σl\sigma_{l} are Pauli spin matrices defined as

σx\displaystyle\sigma_{x} =(0110),σy=(0−ii0),\displaystyle=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\ 1&0\end{array}\right),\quad\sigma_{y}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&-i\\ i&0\end{array}\right),
σz\displaystyle\sigma_{z} =(+100−1).\displaystyle=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}+1&0\\ 0&-1\end{array}\right).

The left-hand side of the inequality given in Eq. (37) is zero for the state

12​(|00⟩+|11⟩).\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|00\rangle+|11\rangle). (44)

We can have a similar construction with only three operators for any system size. Let us consider the usual angular momentum operators jx,jyj_{x},j_{y} and jz,j_{z}, living in a dd-dimensional system, fulfilling

jx2+jy2+jz2=j⁡(j+1)​𝟙,j_{x}^{2}+j_{y}^{2}+j_{z}^{2}=j(j+1)\mathbbm{1}, (45)

where d=2​j+1.d=2j+1. In particular, let us define the matrix [95]

jz=diag⁡(−j,−j+1,…,j−1,j).j_{z}={\rm diag}(-j,-j+1,...,j-1,j). (46)

Then, we need the ladder operators

(j+)m,n=δm,n+1​j⁡(j+1)−(j−n)​(j+1−n)(j_{+})_{m,n}=\delta_{m,n+1}\sqrt{j(j+1)-(j-n)(j+1-n)} (47)

and j−=j+†,j_{-}=j_{+}^{\dagger}, where 1≤m,n≤d1\leq m,n\leq d and δk​l\delta_{kl} is the well-known Kronecker delta. Then, we define the xx and yy components as

jx=j++j−2,jy=j+−j−2​i.j_{x}=\frac{j_{+}+j_{-}}{2},\quad\quad j_{y}=\frac{j_{+}-j_{-}}{2i}. (48)

After clarifying the operators used, we need the uncertainty relation

(Δ​jx)2+(Δ​jy)2+(Δ​jz)2≥j,(\Delta j_{x})^{2}+(\Delta j_{y})^{2}+(\Delta j_{z})^{2}\geq j, (49)

which is true for all quantum states. Based on Eq. (49), it can be proved that for separable states we have [96, 97, 98, 94]

[Δ⁡(jxT⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗jx)]2\displaystyle[\Delta(j_{x}^{T}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes j_{x})]^{2}
+[Δ⁡(jyT⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗jy)]2\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad+[\Delta(j_{y}^{T}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes j_{y})]^{2}
+[Δ⁡(jzT⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗jz)]2≥2​j.\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad+[\Delta(j_{z}^{T}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes j_{z})]^{2}\geq 2j. (50)

c. f. Eq. (37). The left-hand side of the inequality given in Eq. (50) is zero for the maximally entangled state given in Eq. (36). It is easy to see that Eq. (50) is a tight inequality for separable states, since the |+j,+j⟩|+j,+j\rangle state saturates it.

We now present a simple expression for which the maximum for general states is larger than the maximum for separable quantum states. We know that for separable states [99, 97]

⟨(σx⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗σx)2+(σy⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗σy)2⟩≤6,\langle{(\sigma_{x}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes\sigma_{x})^{2}+(\sigma_{y}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes\sigma_{y})^{2}}\rangle\leq 6, (51)

while the maximum for quantum states is 88 and it is taken by the singlet state

12​(|01⟩−|10⟩).\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|01\rangle-|10\rangle). (52)

We add that the product state |01⟩x|01\rangle_{x} saturates the inequality Eq. (51), where |.⟩x|.\rangle_{x} is a state given in the xx-basis. That is, for a qubit, the basis states in the xx-basis are

|0⟩x\displaystyle|0\rangle_{x} =12​(|0⟩+|1⟩),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0\rangle+|1\rangle),
|1⟩x\displaystyle|1\rangle_{x} =12​(|0⟩−|1⟩).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|0\rangle-|1\rangle). (53)

Let us now determine a complementary relation. We will find the minimum for separable states for the left-hand side of Eq. (51). We need to know that for separable states

[Δ⁡(σx⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗σx)]2+[Δ⁡(σy⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗σy)]2≥2[\Delta(\sigma_{x}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes\sigma_{x})]^{2}+[\Delta(\sigma_{y}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes\sigma_{y})]^{2}\geq 2 (54)

holds. This can be seen as follows [91, 92]. We need to know that for two-qubit quantum states

(Δ​σx)2+(Δ​σy)2≥2(\Delta\sigma_{x})^{2}+(\Delta\sigma_{y})^{2}\geq 2 (55)

holds. For product states |Ψ⟩⊗|Φ⟩,|\Psi\rangle\otimes|\Phi\rangle, the left-hand side of Eq. (54) equals the sum of single system variances, which can be bounded from below as

(Δ​σx)Ψ2+(Δ​σy)Ψ2+(Δ​σx)Φ2+(Δ​σy)Φ2≥4.(\Delta\sigma_{x})^{2}_{\Psi}+(\Delta\sigma_{y})^{2}_{\Psi}+(\Delta\sigma_{x})^{2}_{\Phi}+(\Delta\sigma_{y})^{2}_{\Phi}\geq 4. (56)

The bound for separable states given in Eq. (18) is the same as the bound for product states, since the variance is a concave function of the state. The left-hand side of Eq. (54) is zero for the state

12​(|01⟩+|10⟩).\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|01\rangle+|10\rangle). (57)

The product state |11⟩x|11\rangle_{x} saturates the inequality given in Eq. (54) and for that state

⟨σx⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗σx⟩\displaystyle\langle{\sigma_{x}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes\sigma_{x}}\rangle =0,\displaystyle=0,
⟨σy⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗σy⟩\displaystyle\langle{\sigma_{y}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes\sigma_{y}}\rangle =0\displaystyle=0 (58)

hold. Thus, for separable states

⟨(σx⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗σx)2+(σy⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗σy)2⟩≥2\langle{(\sigma_{x}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes\sigma_{x})^{2}+(\sigma_{y}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes\sigma_{y})^{2}}\rangle\geq 2 (59)

holds and it is even a tight inequality for separable states, c. f. Eq. (51).

4 Optimization over the two-copy space

In this section, we first review the formalism that maps the optimization over the decompositions of the density matrix to an optimization of an operator expectation value over bipartite symmetric separable quantum states with given marginals [100] 22 2 For a reference in the literature, see Eq. (67) in Ref. [62] and Eqs. (S23)-(S25) in Ref. [100]. In Eqs. (S23)-(S25) in Ref. [100], there are some additional constraints for the expectation values ⟨Oi⟩ϱ,\langle{O_{i}}\rangle_{\varrho}, where OiO_{i} are some operators. For our discussion, they are not needed.. Then, we show that the same result is obtained if the optimization is carried out over general separable quantum states rather than symmetric separable states.

We start from writing the variance of a pure state |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle as an operator expectation value acting on two copies as

(Δ​H)Ψ2=Tr⁡(Ω⁡|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|⊗|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|),(\Delta H)^{2}_{\Psi}={\rm Tr}(\Omega|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|\otimes|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|), (60)

where we define the operator

Ω=H2⊗𝟙−H⊗H.\Omega=H^{2}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-H\otimes H. (61)

Based on Eq. (60), the expression of the quantum Fisher information given in Eq. (13) can be rewritten as [62, 100]

ℱQ​[ϱ,H]=\displaystyle{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H]=
4​min{pk,|Ψk⟩}\displaystyle 4\min_{\{p_{k},|\Psi_{k}\rangle\}}\; ∑kpk​Tr​[Ω​(|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|)⊗2],\displaystyle\sum_{k}p_{k}{\rm Tr}[\Omega(|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|)^{\otimes 2}],
s. t. ϱ=∑kpk​|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|.\displaystyle\varrho=\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|. (62)

The sum can be moved into the trace and we obtain

ℱQ​[ϱ,H]=\displaystyle{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H]=
4​min{pk,|Ψk⟩}\displaystyle 4\min_{\{p_{k},|\Psi_{k}\rangle\}}\; Tr⁡{Ω⁡[∑kpk​(|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|)⊗2]},\displaystyle{\rm Tr}\left\{\Omega\left[\sum_{k}p_{k}(|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|)^{\otimes 2}\right]\right\},
s. t. ϱ=∑kpk​|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|.\displaystyle\varrho=\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|. (63)

On the right-hand side in Eq. (63) in the square bracket, we can recognize a mixed state living in the two-copy space

ϱ12=∑kpk​|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|⊗|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|,\varrho_{12}=\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|\otimes|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|, (64)

States given in Eq. (64) are symmetric separable states, thus ϱ12∈𝒮′.\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}. We can rewrite the optimization in Eq. (63) as an optmization over symmetric separable states given in Eq. (64) as

ℱQ​[ϱ,H]=minϱ12\displaystyle{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H]=\min_{\varrho_{12}}\; 4​T​r​(Ω​ϱ12),\displaystyle 4{\rm Tr}(\Omega\varrho_{12}),
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒮′,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho. (65)

Due to the optimization over symmetric separable states, Tr1​(ϱ12)=ϱ{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho is fulfilled without adding it as an explicit constraint.

Equation (65) contains an optimization over symmetric separable states, which cannot be computed directly. However, we can consider an optimization over a larger set, the set of symmetric PPT states, which leads to an expression that can be obtained numerically using semidefinite programming [101]

ℱQ(PPT)​[ϱ,H]=minϱ12\displaystyle{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}^{({\rm PPT})}[\varrho,H]=\min_{\varrho_{12}}\; 4​T​r​(Ω​ϱ12),\displaystyle 4{\rm Tr}(\Omega\varrho_{12}),
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒫′,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{P}^{\prime},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho. (66)

In general, the relation

ℱQ(PPT)​[ϱ,H]≤ℱQ​[ϱ,H]{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}^{({\rm PPT})}[\varrho,H]\leq{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H] (67)

holds, while for two qubits we have an equality, since for that system size 𝒮′=𝒫′,\mathcal{S}^{\prime}=\mathcal{P}^{\prime}, as we discussed in Sec. 3.

Let us now change the operator to be optimized, making it permutationally symmetric. Equation (65) can be rewritten as

ℱQ​[ϱ,H]=minϱ12\displaystyle{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H]=\min_{\varrho_{12}}\; 2​T​r​[(H⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗H)2​ϱ12],\displaystyle 2{\rm Tr}[(H\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H)^{2}\varrho_{12}],
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒮′,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho. (68)

We will now show that the expression in Eq. (68) remains true if we change the set over which we have to optimize to the set of separable states.

Observation 1. The quantum Fisher information can be obtained as an optimization over separable states as

ℱQ​[ϱ,H]=minϱ12\displaystyle{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H]=\min_{\varrho_{12}}\; 2​T​r​[(H⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗H)2​ϱ12],\displaystyle 2{\rm Tr}[(H\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H)^{2}\varrho_{12}],
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒮,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱ,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho,
Tr1​(ϱ12)=ϱ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho. (69)

Proof. Using

Tr⁡[(H⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗H)2​ϱ12]\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[(H\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H)^{2}\varrho_{12}]
=2​T​r​(H2​ϱ)−2​T​r​[(H⊗H)​ϱ12],\displaystyle\quad\quad=2{\rm Tr}(H^{2}\varrho)-2{\rm Tr}[(H\otimes H)\varrho_{12}], (70)

the right-hand side of Eq. (69) can be reformulated as

4​T​r​(H2​ϱ)−4​maxϱ12\displaystyle 4{\rm Tr}(H^{2}\varrho)-4\max_{\varrho_{12}}\; Tr⁡[(H⊗H)​ϱ12],\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[(H\otimes H)\varrho_{12}],
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒮,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱ,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho,
Tr1​(ϱ12)=ϱ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho. (71)

Due to the permutational invariance of H⊗HH\otimes H and that both marginals must be equal to ϱ,\varrho, if a separable state given in Eq. (18) maximizes the correlation ⟨H⊗H⟩\langle{H\otimes H}\rangle, then the separable state

∑kpk​|Φk⟩​⟨Φk|⊗|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|.\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Phi_{k}\rangle\langle\Phi_{k}|\otimes|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|. (72)

also maximizes the correlation. Then, the mixture of the above two separable states also maximize the correlation with the given marginals, which can always be written as

ϱ12=∑k=1Mp~k​|Ψ~k⟩​⟨Ψ~k|⊗|Ψ~πk⟩​⟨Ψ~πk|,\varrho_{12}=\sum_{k=1}^{M}\tilde{p}_{k}|\tilde{\Psi}_{k}\rangle\langle\tilde{\Psi}_{k}|\otimes|\tilde{\Psi}_{\pi_{k}}\rangle\langle\tilde{\Psi}_{\pi_{k}}|, (73)

where πk\pi_{k} for k=1,2,..,Mk=1,2,..,M is a permutation of 1,2,…,M1,2,...,M for some M.M. Based on our arguments, it is sufficient to look for the separable state that maximizes ⟨H⊗H⟩\langle{H\otimes H}\rangle in the form Eq. (73), and p~k≥0,\tilde{p}_{k}\geq 0, ∑kp~k=1.\sum_{k}\tilde{p}_{k}=1. Then, the correlation can be given as

Tr⁡[(H⊗H)​ϱ12]=∑k=1Mp~k​hk​hπk,{\rm Tr}[(H\otimes H)\varrho_{12}]=\sum_{k=1}^{M}\tilde{p}_{k}h_{k}h_{\pi_{k}}, (74)

where we define the expectation values of HH on |Ψ~k⟩|\tilde{\Psi}_{k}\rangle as

hk=Tr⁡(H⁡|Ψ~k⟩​⟨Ψ~k|).h_{k}={\rm Tr}(H|\tilde{\Psi}_{k}\rangle\langle\tilde{\Psi}_{k}|). (75)

Based on the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality we have

∑kp~k​hk​hπk\displaystyle\sum_{k}\tilde{p}_{k}h_{k}h_{\pi_{k}} ≤∑kp~k​hk2​∑kp~k​hπk2\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\sum_{k}\tilde{p}_{k}h_{k}^{2}\sum_{k}\tilde{p}_{k}h_{\pi_{k}}^{2}}
≤max⁡(∑kp~k​hk2,∑kp~k​hπk2).\displaystyle\leq\max\left(\sum_{k}\tilde{p}_{k}h_{k}^{2},\sum_{k}\tilde{p}_{k}h_{\pi_{k}}^{2}\right). (76)

Thus, when we maximize Tr⁡[(H⊗H)​ϱ12]{\rm Tr}[(H\otimes H)\varrho_{12}] over separable states with the constraints for the marginals, the maximum is taken by a symmetric separable state given in Eq. (64). In this case both inequalities are saturated in Eq. (76). ■\hfill\blacksquare

Based on Eq. (15), we can obtain the variance also as a result of an optimization over a two-copy space.

Observation 2. The variance can also be obtained as an optimization over symmetric separable states as

(Δ​H)2=maxϱ12\displaystyle(\Delta H)^{2}=\max_{\varrho_{12}}\; 12​Tr​[(H⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗H)2​ϱ12],\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}[(H\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H)^{2}\varrho_{12}],
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒮′,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱ,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho,
Tr1​(ϱ12)=ϱ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho. (77)

Example 1. Note that if we replace the set of symmetric separable states by the set of separable states in Eq. (77), then we get a different quantity, which can be larger in some cases than (Δ​H)2.(\Delta H)^{2}. Let us see a concrete example. For instance, if ϱ=𝟙/2\varrho=\mathbbm{1}/2 then among symmetric separable states, the maximum is 11 and it is attained by the state

ϱ12=14​(|00⟩​⟨00|+|11⟩​⟨11|+2|Ψ+⟩​⟨Ψ+|),\varrho_{12}=\frac{1}{4}\left(|00\rangle\langle 00|+|11\rangle\langle 11|+2|\Psi^{+}\rangle\langle\Psi^{+}|\right), (78)

where the Bell state |Ψ+⟩|\Psi^{+}\rangle is given as

|Ψ+⟩=12​(|01⟩+|10⟩).|\Psi^{+}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|01\rangle+|10\rangle). (79)

The state given in Eq. (78) can be decomposed into the mixture of symmetric product states as

14​(|α+1⟩​⟨α+1|+|α−1⟩​⟨α−1|+|α+i⟩​⟨α+i|+|α−i⟩​⟨α−i|),\frac{1}{4}(|\alpha_{+1}\rangle\langle\alpha_{+1}|+|\alpha_{-1}\rangle\langle\alpha_{-1}|+|\alpha_{+i}\rangle\langle\alpha_{+i}|+|\alpha_{-i}\rangle\langle\alpha_{-i}|), (80)

where the symmetric product state is defined as

|αq⟩=(|0⟩+q⁡|1⟩)⊗(|0⟩+q⁡|1⟩).|\alpha_{q}\rangle=(|0\rangle+q|1\rangle)\otimes(|0\rangle+q|1\rangle). (81)

Among separable states, the maximum is 22 and it is attained by the state

ϱ12=12​(|01⟩​⟨01|+|10⟩​⟨10|).\varrho_{12}=\frac{1}{2}\left(|01\rangle\langle 01|+|10\rangle\langle 10|\right). (82)

Note that ϱ12\varrho_{12} given in Eq. (82) is not symmetric.

5 Quantum Wasserstein distance based on a separable coupling

Next, we will connect our result in Observation 4 to results available in the literature mentioned in the introduction. We will consider the quantum Wasserstein distance such that the optimization takes place over separable states rather than over general bipartite quantum states. We will consider such modifications of DGMPC​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} and DDPT​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, and examine their properties.

Our first finding concerning the GMPC distance is the following.

Definition 3. Modifying the definition in Eq. (5) we can define a new type of GMPC distance such that we restrict the optimization over separable states as

DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2\displaystyle D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\quad
=12minϱ12∑n=1N\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\min_{\varrho_{12}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\; Tr⁡[(Hn⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Hn)2​ϱ12],\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[(H_{n}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H_{n})^{2}\varrho_{12}],
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒮,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S},
Tr1​(ϱ12)=ϱ,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho,
Tr2​(ϱ12)=σ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\sigma. (83)

We can see immediately two relevant properties of the newly defined distance. Observation 4 showed that for N=1N=1 for a given H1H_{1}

DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,ϱ)2=14​ℱQ​[ϱ,H1]D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\varrho)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H_{1}] (84)

holds. Moreover, based on Eqs. (5) and (83), we can immediately see that

DGMPC​(ϱ,σ)2≤DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\leq D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, (85)

since on the left-hand side of Eq. (85) there is a minimization over a larger set of quantum states than on the right-hand side. Based on Eqs. (84) and (85), it follows that for the self-distance for N=1N=1 for a given H1H_{1} we obtain

DGMPC​(ϱ,ϱ)2≤14​ℱQ​[ϱ,H1].D_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\varrho)^{2}\leq\frac{1}{4}{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H_{1}]. (86)

Now, our goal is to give an optimal transport map (plan) corresponding to an optimal coupling of DG​M​P​C,sep​(ϱ,σ)2.D_{GMPC,\rm sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}. Note that there can be several optimal couplings. We look for a CPTP map Φ\Phi corresponding to an optimal separable coupling ϱ12.\varrho_{12}. Let us assume that an optimal separable coupling equals the separable state given in Eq. (18). Based on Definition 5, it has the following marginals. We obtain ϱ\varrho as in Eq. (14), and for the state σ\sigma

σ=∑kpk​|Φk⟩​⟨Φk|,\sigma=\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Phi_{k}\rangle\langle\Phi_{k}|, (87)

holds. Let us consider the map [46]

Φ⁡(X)=∑kBk​X​Bk†.\Phi(X)=\sum_{k}B_{k}XB_{k}^{\dagger}. (88)

where the Kraus operators are given as

Bk=pkAkϱ−1/2,B_{k}=\sqrt{p_{k}}A_{k}\varrho^{-1/2}, (89)

and ϱ−1\varrho^{-1} is the inverse of ϱ\varrho on its support.

For our particular transport problem, let us choose

Ak=|Φk⟩​⟨Ψk|.A_{k}=|\Phi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|. (90)

It is clear that Φ\Phi is completely positive and it is trace preserving, since

∑kBk†​Bk\displaystyle\sum_{k}B_{k}^{\dagger}B_{k} =∑kpkϱ−1/2|Ψk⟩⟨Φk|Φk⟩⟨Ψk|ϱ−1/2\displaystyle=\sum_{k}p_{k}\varrho^{-1/2}|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Phi_{k}|\Phi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|\varrho^{-1/2}
=ϱ−1/2∑kpk|Ψk⟩⟨Ψk|ϱ−1/2\displaystyle=\varrho^{-1/2}\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|\varrho^{-1/2}
=ϱ−1/2ϱϱ−1/2=𝟙.\displaystyle=\varrho^{-1/2}\varrho\varrho^{-1/2}=\mathbbm{1}. (91)

Since the map transforms ϱ\varrho to σ\sigma

Φ⁡(ϱ)\displaystyle\Phi(\varrho) =∑kpk|Φk⟩⟨Ψk|ϱ−1/2ϱϱ−1/2|Ψk⟩⟨Φk|pk\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\sqrt{p_{k}}|\Phi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|\varrho^{-1/2}\varrho\varrho^{-1/2}|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Phi_{k}|\sqrt{p_{k}}
=∑kpk​|Φk⟩​⟨Φk|=σ,\displaystyle=\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Phi_{k}\rangle\langle\Phi_{k}|=\sigma, (92)

the CPTP map Φ\Phi given in Eq. (88) gives the optimal transport map we were looking for.

Let us see some properties of the map we have just found. If |Ψk⟩|\Psi_{k}\rangle are pairwise orthogonal to each other then

Bk=Ak=|Φk⟩​⟨Ψk|B_{k}=A_{k}=|\Phi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}| (93)

holds. In this case, the map can be realized by a von Neumann measurement in the basis given by {|Ψk⟩},\{|\Psi_{k}\rangle\}, with a subsequent unitary that transforms |Ψk⟩|\Psi_{k}\rangle to |Φk⟩.|\Phi_{k}\rangle. It is instructive to look at the action of the map on the state

ϱ0=∑kpk​|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|1⊗|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|2.\varrho_{0}=\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|_{1}\otimes|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|_{2}. (94)

Then, we obtain the optimal coupling ϱ12\varrho_{12} as

(𝟙⊗Φ)​(ϱ0)=∑kpk​|Ψk⟩​⟨Ψk|1⊗|Φk⟩​⟨Φk|2.(\mathbbm{1}\otimes\Phi)(\varrho_{0})=\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Psi_{k}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}|_{1}\otimes|\Phi_{k}\rangle\langle\Phi_{k}|_{2}. (95)

Hence, for every map of given by Eqs. (88), (89) and (90) there is a corresponding coupling.

In summary, if we restrict the optimization for separable states, then when computing DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, for all ϱ\varrho and σ,\sigma, there is a transport map corresponding to all optimal couplings. Note that this was not the case for DGMPC​(ϱ,σ)2.D_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}.

Let us now define another distance based on an optimization over separable states.

Definition 4. Based on the definition of DDPT​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} given in Eq. (1), we can also define

DDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)2\displaystyle D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\quad\quad\quad
=12minϱ12∑n=1N\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\min_{\varrho_{12}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\; Tr⁡[(HnT⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Hn)2​ϱ12],\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[(H_{n}^{T}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H_{n})^{2}\varrho_{12}],
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒮,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱT,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho^{T},
Tr1​(ϱ12)=σ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\sigma. (96)

As an important property of DDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, we can see that

DDPT​(ϱ,σ)2≤DDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\leq D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} (97)

holds, since on the left-hand side of Eq. (97) there is a minimization over a larger set of quantum states than on the right-hand side.

Let us see now, what kind of map corresponds to an optimal separable coupling ϱ12,\varrho_{12}, when we calculate DDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)2.D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}. Let us assume that an optimal separable coupling is of the form

ϱ12=∑kpk​|Ψk∗⟩​⟨Ψk∗|1⊗|Φk⟩​⟨Φk|2.\varrho_{12}=\sum_{k}p_{k}|\Psi_{k}^{*}\rangle\langle\Psi_{k}^{*}|_{1}\otimes|\Phi_{k}\rangle\langle\Phi_{k}|_{2}. (98)

Based on Definition 5, we obtain ϱ\varrho as in Eq. (14), and σ\sigma as in Eq. (87). It turns out that the map we need is just Φ⁡(ϱ)\Phi(\varrho) defined in Eq. (88). It is instructive to look at the action of the map on the state

Hence, for every map of given by Eqs. (88), (89) and (90) there is a corresponding coupling.

It is instructive to relate our results to those of Ref. [46]. In Ref. [46], the role of ϱ0T1\varrho_{0}^{T_{1}} is played by the purification. Moreover, if we compute the self-distance and thus ϱ=σ,\varrho=\sigma, the map given in Eq. (88) is not the identity map. On the other hand, in Ref. [46] the map was the identity map in that case.

Interestingly, the two different distance measures, defined with the transpose and without it, respectively, are equal to each other.

It is possible to prove that the two new quantities are equal to each other.

Observation 5. The two quantum Wasserstein distance measures are equal to each other

DDPT,PPT​(ϱ,σ)2=DGMPC,PPT​(ϱ,σ)2.D_{\rm DPT,PPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}=D_{\rm GMPC,PPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}. (139)

Proof. We have to follow ideas similar to the ones in Observation 5. In particular, we need to use that ϱ12\varrho_{12} is a PPT quantum state if and only if ϱ12T1\varrho_{12}^{T_{1}} is a PPT quantum state.■\hfill\blacksquare

In order to define further Wasserstein distance measures based on an optimization over other supersets of separable states, we need to know the separability criterion based on symmetric extensions [105, 106, 107]. A given bipartite state ϱA​B\varrho_{AB} is said to have a n:mn:m symmetric extension if it can be written as the reduced state of a multipartite state ϱA1..An​B1..Bm,\varrho_{A_{1}..A_{n}B_{1}..B_{m}}, which is symmetric under Ak↔AlA_{k}\leftrightarrow A_{l} for all k≠lk\neq l and under Bk′↔Bl′B_{k^{\prime}}\leftrightarrow B_{l^{\prime}} for all k′≠l′.k^{\prime}\neq l^{\prime}. If we also require that the state is PPT for all bipartitions, then the state has a PPT symmetric extension. The requirement of having a PPT symmetric extension for n=1n=1 and m=1m=1 is equivalent to the PPT condition, while for n>1n>1 or m>1m>1 the condition is stronger. Bipartite separable states have such extensions for arbitrarily large nn and m,m, while the lack of such an extension for some mm and nn signals the presence of entanglement. In particular, a state is separable if and only if there is an extension for any nn and for m=1.m=1.

Let us define DDPT,PPT​n​(ϱ,σ)2D_{{\rm DPT,PPT}n}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} and DGMPC,PPT​n​(ϱ,σ)2D_{{\rm GMPC,PPT}n}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} based on an optimization over quantum states with a PPT symmetric extension for given nn and for m=1.m=1.

DDPT,PPT​n​(ϱ,σ)2≤DDPT,PPT​n′​(ϱ,σ)2D_{{\rm DPT,PPT}n}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\leq D_{{\rm DPT,PPT}n^{\prime}}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} (140)

if n′>n.n^{\prime}>n. Based on Observations 5 and 5, we can also see that

DDPT,PPT​n​(ϱ,σ)2=DGMPC,PPT​n​(ϱ,σ)2D_{{\rm DPT,PPT}n}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}=D_{{\rm GMPC,PPT}n}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} (141)

for every n.n.

6 Variance-like quantities

When we compare the expression in Eq. (68) defining the quantum Fisher information and the other expression in Eq. (77) defining the variance, we can see that the main difference is that the minimization is replaced by a maximization. We also showed a similar relation between the entanglement of formation given in Eq. (27), and the entanglement of assistance given in Eq. (29). Based on this observation, we can define variance-like quantities from the various forms of quantum Wasserstein distance by replacing the minimization by maximization.

Such a variance-like quantity can be interpreted in the framework of transport problems as follows. The quantum Wasserstein distance determines the smallest cost possible for the transport problem by a minimization. The variance-like quantities presented in this section determine the largest cost possible for the transport problem. Knowing the largest possible cost is useful when judging how close the cost of a given transport plan is to the optimal cost.

Let us now define the first variance-like quantity.

Definition 5. From the GMPC distance with an optimization restricted over separable states given in Eq. (83), we obtain the following variance like quantity

VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)\displaystyle V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)\quad\quad\quad
=12maxϱ12∑n=1N\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\max_{\varrho_{12}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\; Tr⁡[(Hn⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Hn)2​ϱ12],\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[(H_{n}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H_{n})^{2}\varrho_{12}],
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒮,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱ,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho,
Tr1​(ϱ12)=σ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\sigma. (142)

Clearly, the inequality

VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)≥DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)\geq D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} (143)

holds, since since on the left-hand side of Eq. (143) we maximize over a set of quantum states while on the right-hand side we minimize over the same set.

We can define analogously VDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ),V_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma), VGMPC​(ϱ,σ),V_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma), and VDPT​(ϱ,σ),V_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma), modifying the definition of DDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, DGMPC​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, and DDPT​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, respectively. In all these cases, a relation analogous to the one in Eq. (143) can be obtained.

The value of VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma) is related to the variance.

Observation 6. The GMPC variance defined in Eq. (142) is bounded from below as

VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)≥12​∑n=1N(Δ​Hn)ϱ2+(Δ​Hn)σ2.V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)\geq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\varrho}+(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\sigma}. (144)

Proof. We can rewrite the expression to be computed for VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma) as

12​max⁡∑n=1Nϱ12∈𝒮⁡Tr⁡[(Hn⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Hn)2​ϱ12]\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\max_{\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S}}\;\sum_{n=1}^{N}{\rm Tr}[(H_{n}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H_{n})^{2}\varrho_{12}]
=12​∑n=1N(Δ​Hn)ϱ2+(Δ​Hn)σ2+(⟨Hn⟩ϱ−⟨Hn⟩σ)2\displaystyle\quad\quad=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\varrho}+(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\sigma}+(\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\varrho}-\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\sigma})^{2}
−minϱ12∈𝒮⁡Cϱ12,\displaystyle\quad\quad-\min_{\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S}}\;C_{\varrho_{12}}, (145)

where ϱ12\varrho_{12} has marginals ϱ\varrho and σ,\sigma, as given in Eq. (128), and we define

Cϱ12=∑n=1N⟨Hn⊗Hn⟩ϱ12−⟨Hn⟩ϱ​⟨Hn⟩σ.C_{\varrho_{12}}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\langle{H_{n}\otimes H_{n}}\rangle_{\varrho_{12}}-\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\varrho}\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\sigma}. (146)

Since the product state ϱ⊗σ\varrho\otimes\sigma is separable and fulfills the conditions on the marginals, it is clear that

minϱ12∈𝒮⁡Cϱ12≤Cϱ⊗σ=0.\min_{\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S}}C_{\varrho_{12}}\leq C_{\varrho\otimes\sigma}=0. (147)

Substituting Eq. (147) into Eq. (145), using the fact (⟨Hn⟩ϱ−⟨Hn⟩σ)2≥0,(\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\varrho}-\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\sigma})^{2}\geq 0, we can prove the observation. ■\hfill\blacksquare

We can even obtain an upper bound.

Observation 7. The GMPC variance defined in Eq. (142) is bounded from above as

VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)\displaystyle V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma) ≤∑n=1N(Δ​Hn)ϱ2+(Δ​Hn)σ2\displaystyle\leq\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\varrho}+(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\sigma}
+⟨Hn⟩ϱ2+⟨Hn⟩σ2.\displaystyle+\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\varrho}^{2}+\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\sigma}^{2}. (148)

Proof. We can find an upper bound for the expression to be computed for VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma) as

12​max⁡∑n=1Nϱ12∈𝒮⁡Tr⁡[(Hn⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Hn)2​ϱ12]\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\max_{\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S}}\;\sum_{n=1}^{N}{\rm Tr}[(H_{n}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H_{n})^{2}\varrho_{12}]
≤∑n=1N⟨Hn2⟩ϱ+⟨Hn2⟩σ,\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\leq\sum_{n=1}^{N}\langle{H_{n}^{2}}\rangle_{\varrho}+\langle{H_{n}^{2}}\rangle_{\sigma}, (149)

where ϱ12\varrho_{12} has marginals ϱ\varrho and σ,\sigma, as given in Eq. (128), and we used that

Hn2⊗𝟙+𝟙⊗Hn2≥2​Hn⊗Hn.H_{n}^{2}\otimes\mathbbm{1}+\mathbbm{1}\otimes H_{n}^{2}\geq 2H_{n}\otimes H_{n}. (150)

■\hfill\blacksquare

Let us see some concrete examples.

Example 6. Interestingly, the quantity

𝒱:=VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)\mathcal{V}:=V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma) (151)

can be larger or smaller than or equal to

𝒱¯:=12​[VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,ϱ)+VGMPC,sep​(σ,σ)],\overline{\mathcal{V}}:=\frac{1}{2}\left[V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\varrho)+V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\sigma,\sigma)\right], (152)

c. f. Eq. (5). We consider N=1N=1 and H1=σz.H_{1}=\sigma_{z}. The three possibilities above are realized by the following states. For the state

ϱ\displaystyle\varrho =|0⟩​⟨0|,\displaystyle=|0\rangle\langle 0|,
σ\displaystyle\sigma =diag⁡(0.25,0.75),\displaystyle={\rm diag}(0.25,0.75), (153)

we have 𝒱>𝒱¯.\mathcal{V}>\overline{\mathcal{V}}. For the following state

ϱ\displaystyle\varrho =|0⟩​⟨0|,\displaystyle=|0\rangle\langle 0|,
σ\displaystyle\sigma =diag⁡(0.75,0.25),\displaystyle={\rm diag}(0.75,0.25), (154)

ϱ\displaystyle\varrho =𝟙/2,\displaystyle=\mathbbm{1}/2,
σ\displaystyle\sigma =(0.750.400.400.25),\displaystyle=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0.75&0.40\\ 0.40&0.25\end{array}\right),

ϱ\displaystyle\varrho =𝟙/3,\displaystyle=\mathbbm{1}/3,
σ\displaystyle\sigma =diag⁡(1,0,0),\displaystyle={\rm diag}(1,0,0), (157)

we have 𝒱<𝒱¯.\mathcal{V}<\overline{\mathcal{V}}. Note that in all examples where ϱ,σ\varrho,\sigma and H1H_{1} were all diagonal, there is an optimal diagonal ϱ12,\varrho_{12}, essentially corresponding to the classical case.

The two different variance-like quantities, defined with the transpose and without it, respectively, are equal to each other.

Observation 8. The two types of quantum Wasserstein variance are equal to each other

VDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)=VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ).V_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)=V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma). (158)

Proof. The proof is analogous to that of Observation 5. ■\hfill\blacksquare

Let us calculate VDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)V_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma) for some concrete examples.

Example 7. Let us consider the case when ϱ=|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|\varrho=|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi| is a pure state of any dimension and σ\sigma is an arbitrary density matrix of the same dimension. Then, when computing the various types of quantum Wasserstein distance and quantum Wasserstein variance between ϱ\varrho and σ,\sigma, the state ϱ12\varrho_{12} in the optimization is constrained to be the tensor product of the two density matrices. Hence, it follows that

VDPT​(|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|,σ)=DDPT​(|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|,σ)2V_{\rm DPT}(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|,\sigma)=D_{\rm DPT}(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|,\sigma)^{2} (159)

holds, and analogous equations hold for the quantities VDPT,sep​(|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|,σ),VGMPC,sep​(|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|,σ),V_{\rm DPT,sep}(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|,\sigma),V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|,\sigma), and VGMPC​(|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|,σ),V_{\rm GMPC}(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|,\sigma), where the Wasserstein distance measures for this case are given in Eq. ().

Example 8. For ϱ=σ=|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|,\varrho=\sigma=|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|, and for N=1N=1 for a given H1H_{1} we obtain

VDPT​(|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|,|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|)=(Δ​H1)Ψ2.V_{\rm DPT}(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|,|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|)=(\Delta H_{1})^{2}_{\Psi}. (160)

Example 9. Let us consider the single-qubit states given in Eq. (111). Let us take N=1N=1 and H1=σz.H_{1}=\sigma_{z}. Then, when computing VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ),V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma), the optimum is attained by the separable state

ϱ12=12​|01⟩​⟨01|+12|10⟩​⟨10|,\varrho_{12}=\frac{1}{2}|01\rangle\langle 01|+\frac{1}{2}|10\rangle\langle 10|, (161)

[c. f. Eq. (112)] and we have

VGMPC,sep​(12​𝟙,12​𝟙)=2.V_{\rm GMPC,sep}\left(\frac{1}{2}\mathbbm{1},\frac{1}{2}\mathbbm{1}\right)=2. (162)

(See also Example 4.) If H1H_{1} is a different operator then the state ϱ12\varrho_{12} corresponding to the maximum will be different. It can be obtained from the state given in Eq. (161) with local unitaries. For instance, for H1=σx,H_{1}=\sigma_{x}, the optimum is reached by the separable state

ϱ12=12​|01⟩​⟨01|x+12|10⟩​⟨10|x,\varrho_{12}=\frac{1}{2}|01\rangle\langle 01|_{x}+\frac{1}{2}|10\rangle\langle 10|_{x}, (163)

where |.⟩x|.\rangle_{x} is a state given in the xx-basis.

7 Quantum Wasserstein distance and entanglement criteria

Example 5 highlighted that in certain cases the minimum for separable states is larger than the minimum for general states. In this case, entanglement can help to decrease the quantum Wasserstein distance. In this section, we analyze the relation of the quantum Wasserstein distance and entanglement conditions on the optimal ϱ12\varrho_{12} couplings.

First, we make the following simple observation.

Observation 9. If

DDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)2>DDPT​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}>D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} (164)

holds then all ϱ12\varrho_{12} states that minimize the cost for a given ϱ\varrho and σ,\sigma, when computing DDPT​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, are entangled. In short, all optimal ϱ12\varrho_{12} states are entangled. The situation is analogous if

DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2>DGMPC​(ϱ,σ)2.D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}>D_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}. (165)

Then, all optimal ϱ12\varrho_{12} states for a given ϱ\varrho and σ,\sigma, when computing DGMPC​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, are entangled. Thus, we can even use the quantum Wasserstein distance as an entanglement criterion detecting entanglement in the optimal ϱ12\varrho_{12} states.

We can even consider conditions with the self-distance. Based on Eqs. (3), (84), and (101), we find that for the N=1N=1 case

DDPT,sep​(ϱ,ϱ)2>DDPT​(ϱ,ϱ)2D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\varrho)^{2}>D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\varrho)^{2} (166)

is equivalent to a relation between the quantum Fisher information and the Wigner-Yanase skew information

FQ​[ϱ,H1]4>Iϱ​(H1).\frac{F_{Q}[\varrho,H_{1}]}{4}>I_{\varrho}(H_{1}). (167)

Thus, the condition in Eq. (167) implies that the optimal ϱ12\varrho_{12} states, obtained when computing DDPT​(ϱ,ϱ)2,D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\varrho)^{2}, are all entangled.

Let us now use entanglement criteria to construct relations for the quantum Wasserstein distance, that can verify that the coupling ϱ12\varrho_{12} is entangled. If the inequality given in Eq. (35) holds for separable states, so does the inequality

∑n=1d2−1⟨(GnT⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Gn)2⟩≥4​(d−1),\sum_{n=1}^{d^{2}-1}\langle{(G_{n}^{T}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes G_{n})^{2}}\rangle\geq 4(d-1), (168)

since the left-hand side of Eq. (168) is never smaller than the left-hand side of Eq. (35). Any state that violates the inequality in Eq. (168) is entangled. It can be shown that Eq. (168) is a tight inequality for separable states as follows. Based on Eq. (34), we see that for pure product states of the form

(|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|)T⊗|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|,(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|)^{T}\otimes|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|, (169)

for the second moments

∑n=1d2−1⟨(GnT⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Gn)2⟩=4​(d−1)\sum_{n=1}^{d^{2}-1}\langle{(G_{n}^{T}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes G_{n})^{2}}\rangle=4(d-1) (170)

holds since for this state

⟨GnT⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Gn⟩=0\langle{G_{n}^{T}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes G_{n}}\rangle=0 (171)

for all n.n.

Next, we will define a quantum Wasserstein distance related to the entanglement condition in Eq. (168).

Observation 10. Let us consider dd-dimensional systems with

Hn=GnH_{n}=G_{n} (172)

for n=1,2,…,d2−1.n=1,2,...,d^{2}-1. If

DDPT{G1,G2,…,Gd2−1}​(ϱ,σ)2<2​(d−1)D_{\rm DPT}^{\{G_{1},G_{2},...,G_{d^{2}-1}\}}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}<2(d-1) (173)

holds, then all optimal ϱ12\varrho_{12} states are entangled. Here, for clarity, we give explicitly the observables used to define the distance in the superscript.

Clearly, since when calculating DDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, we optimize over separable states, we have

DDPT,sep{G1,G2,…,Gd2−1}​(ϱ,σ)2≥2​(d−1).D_{\rm DPT,sep}^{\{G_{1},G_{2},...,G_{d^{2}-1}\}}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\geq 2(d-1). (174)

Thus, independently from what ϱ\varrho and σ\sigma are, their distance DDPT,sep{G1,G2,…,Gd2−1}​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm DPT,sep}^{\{G_{1},G_{2},...,G_{d^{2}-1}\}}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} cannot be smaller than a bound. This is true even if ϱ=σ.\varrho=\sigma.

Let us now use another entanglement condition to construct relations for the quantum Wasserstein distance that can verify that the coupling is entangled. We know that the inequality given in Eq. (50) holds for separable states and it is tight. Based on these, we can obtain the following bounds on the quantum Wasserstein distance.

Observation 11. Let us choose the set of operators as

{Hn}={jx,jy,jz}.\{H_{n}\}=\{j_{x},j_{y},j_{z}\}. (175)

Then, if the inequality

DDPT{jx,jy,jz}​(ϱ,σ)2<jD_{\rm DPT}^{\{j_{x},j_{y},j_{z}\}}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}<j (176)

holds, then all optimal ϱ12\varrho_{12} states are entangled.

Clearly, since when calculating DDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, we optimize over separable states, we have

DDPT,sep{jx,jy,jz}​(ϱ,σ)2≥j.D^{\{j_{x},j_{y},j_{z}\}}_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\geq j. (177)

Thus, again, independently from what ϱ\varrho and σ\sigma are, their distance DDPT,sep{jx,jy,jz}​(ϱ,σ)2D^{\{j_{x},j_{y},j_{z}\}}_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} cannot be smaller than a bound. This is true even if ϱ=σ.\varrho=\sigma.

So far we studied the relation of the quantum Wasserstein distance to entanglement. Next, let us consider the relation of VDPT​(ϱ,σ)V_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma) and VGMPC​(ϱ,σ)V_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma) to entanglement.

Observation 12. If

VDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)<VDPT​(ϱ,σ)V_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)<V_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma) (178)

holds then all optimal ϱ12\varrho_{12} states for a given ϱ\varrho and σ,\sigma, when computing VDPT​(ϱ,σ),V_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma), are entangled. The situation is analogous if

VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)<VGMPC​(ϱ,σ).V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)<V_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma). (179)

Next, we will determine a set of HnH_{n} operators that can be used efficiently to detect entanglement with the quantum Wasserstein variance. For that, we need to know that for separable states the inequality given in Eq. (51) holds.

Observation 13. Let us consider an example with d=2d=2 and {Hn}={σx,σy}.\{H_{n}\}=\{\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}\}. If the condition

VGMPC{σx,σy}​(ϱ,σ)>3V_{\rm GMPC}^{\{\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}\}}(\varrho,\sigma)>3 (180)

holds, then all optimal ϱ12\varrho_{12} states are entangled. Clearly, since when calculating VDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ),V_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma), we optimize over separable states, we have

VGMPC,sep{σx,σy}​(ϱ,σ)≤3.V_{\rm GMPC,sep}^{\{\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}\}}(\varrho,\sigma)\leq 3. (181)

Let us see now a complementary relation for DGMPC​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} and DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2.D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}. They will use the same HnH_{n} operators that appear in Observation 7. We need to know that for separable states the inequality given in Eq. (59) holds.

Observation 14. Let us consider d=2d=2 and {Hn}={σx,σy}.\{H_{n}\}=\{\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}\}. If

DGMPC{σx,σy}​(ϱ,σ)2<1D_{\rm GMPC}^{\{\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}\}}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}<1 (182)

then all optimal ϱ12\varrho_{12} states are entangled. Clearly, since when calculating DDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ),D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma), we optimize over separable states, we have

DGMPC,sep{σx,σy}​(ϱ,σ)2≥1.D_{\rm GMPC,sep}^{\{\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y}\}}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\geq 1. (183)

Statements analogous to those of Observations 7 and 7 can be formulated, with identical bounds, for VDPT​(ϱ,σ)2,V_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, VDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)2,V_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, DDPT​(ϱ,σ)2,D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}, and DDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)2.D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}.

8 Optimization of the variance over the two-copy space

In this section, we examine the quantity that we obtain after replacing the second moment by a variance in the optimization in the definition of DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} given in Eq. (83) and in the definition of VGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)V_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma) in Eq. (142). Analogous ideas work also for the other types of quantum Wasserstein distance and quantum Wasserstein variance defined before. We will show that such quantities have interesting properties.

Definition 6. After replacing the second moment by a variance in the optimization in the definition of DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} given in Eq. (83), we define

D~GMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2\displaystyle\tilde{D}_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\quad\quad\quad
=12minϱ12∑n=1N\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\min_{\varrho_{12}}\;\sum_{n=1}^{N}\; [Δ⁡(Hn⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Hn)]ϱ122,\displaystyle[\Delta(H_{n}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H_{n})]^{2}_{\varrho_{12}},
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒮,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱ,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho,
Tr1​(ϱ12)=σ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\sigma. (184)

Let us see some properties of the quantity we have just introduced. In general, for mixed states,

D~GMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2\displaystyle\tilde{D}_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} =DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2\displaystyle=D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}
−12∑n(⟨Hn⟩ϱ−⟨Hn⟩σ)2\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n}(\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\varrho}-\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\sigma})^{2}

holds, hence clearly

D~GMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2≤DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2.\tilde{D}_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\leq D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}. (186)

Due to the relation in Eq. (8), for the self-distance we have

D~GMPC,sep​(ϱ,ϱ)2=DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,ϱ)2,\tilde{D}_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\varrho)^{2}=D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\varrho)^{2}, (187)

where DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} is given in Eq. (83).

We can write the expression to be optimized as

∑n=1N[Δ⁡(Hn⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Hn)]ϱ122\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}[\Delta(H_{n}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H_{n})]^{2}_{\varrho_{12}}
=∑n=1N[(Δ​Hn)ϱ2+(Δ​Hn)σ2]−2​Cϱ12,\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad=\sum_{n=1}^{N}[(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\varrho}+(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\sigma}]-2C_{\varrho_{12}}, (188)

where ϱ12\varrho_{12} has marginals ϱ\varrho and σ,\sigma, as given in Eq. (128), and we define Cϱ12C_{\varrho_{12}} as in Eq. (146). For pure states, ϱ=|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|\varrho=|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi| and σ=|Φ⟩​⟨Φ|\sigma=|\Phi\rangle\langle\Phi|, we have C=0,C=0, and hence

D~GMPC,sep​(|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|,|Φ⟩​⟨Φ|)2\displaystyle\tilde{D}_{\rm GMPC,sep}(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|,|\Phi\rangle\langle\Phi|)^{2}
=12[D~GMPC,sep(|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|,|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|)2\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad=\frac{1}{2}\bigg[\tilde{D}_{\rm GMPC,sep}(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|,|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|)^{2}
+D~GMPC,sep(|Φ⟩⟨Φ|,|Φ⟩⟨Φ|)2].\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad+\tilde{D}_{\rm GMPC,sep}(|\Phi\rangle\langle\Phi|,|\Phi\rangle\langle\Phi|)^{2}\bigg]. (189)

We can present lower bounds on the distance.

Observation 15. The modified GMPC distance defined in Eq. (184) is bounded from below as

D~GMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2≥18​∑n=1NℱQ​[ϱ,Hn]+18​∑n=1NℱQ​[σ,Hn],\tilde{D}_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}\geq\frac{1}{8}\sum_{n=1}^{N}{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\varrho,H_{n}]+\frac{1}{8}\sum_{n=1}^{N}{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}[\sigma,H_{n}], (190)

while for ϱ=σ\varrho=\sigma we have equality for N=1N=1 in Eq. (190).

Proof. We can rewrite the optimization problem in Eq. (184) based on Eqs. (127) and (8) as

D~GMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2\displaystyle\tilde{D}_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}
=12min{pk,|Ψk⟩,|Φk⟩}∑n=1N∑kpk[(ΔHn)Ψk2+(ΔHn)Φk2\displaystyle\quad=\frac{1}{2}\min_{\{p_{k},|\Psi_{k}\rangle,|\Phi_{k}\rangle\}}\;\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{k}p_{k}\bigg[(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\Psi_{k}}+(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\Phi_{k}}
+(⟨Hn⟩Ψk−⟨Hn⟩Φk)2−(⟨Hn⟩ϱ−⟨Hn⟩σ)2]\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad+\left(\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\Psi_{k}}-\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\Phi_{k}}\right)^{2}-\left(\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\varrho}-\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\sigma}\right)^{2}\bigg]
≥12[min{pk,|Ψk⟩}∑n=1N∑kpk(ΔHn)Ψk2\displaystyle\quad\geq\frac{1}{2}\bigg[\min_{\{p_{k},|\Psi_{k}\rangle\}}\;\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{k}p_{k}(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\Psi_{k}}

9 Optimization over other subsets of physical states

So far we considered Wasserstein distance based on an optimization over all bipartite physical states, separable states, PPT states, and states with a PPT symmetric extension considered in Sec. 5. In this section we examine other convex sets of quantum states. We will also discuss some relevant couplings. By optimizing over a convex set different from the ones we have considered, we will obtain a Wasserstein distance with a different self-distance.

Let us consider the set of couplings for which the quantum discord is zero [108, 109, 110]. If we assume that

Tr2​(ϱ12)\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12}) =ϱ,\displaystyle=\varrho,
Tr1​(ϱ12)\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12}) =σ\displaystyle=\sigma (198)

hold, then an element of the set is of the form

ϱ12=∑kλk​|k⟩​⟨k|⊗σk,\varrho_{12}=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}|k\rangle\langle k|\otimes\sigma_{k}, (199)

where the eigendecomposition of ϱ\varrho is given in Eq. (9) and

σ=∑kλk​σk.\sigma=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\sigma_{k}. (200)

Clearly, such states given in Eq. (199) form a convex set. Such states are called classical-quantum since in subsystem 11 we have a mixture of states that are pairwise orthogonal to each other [110]. We will denote the set of such states as 𝒞1.\mathcal{C}_{1}. For such couplings, the map given in Eq. (88) needs only a von Neumann measurement.

Another possibility is the quantum-classical states, which we will denote by 𝒞2.\mathcal{C}_{2}. Such states are of the form

∑kλk′​ϱk⊗|k′⟩​⟨k′|,\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}^{\prime}\varrho_{k}\otimes|k^{\prime}\rangle\langle k^{\prime}|, (201)

where the eigendecomposition of σ\sigma is

σ=∑kλk′​|k′⟩​⟨k′|,\sigma=\sum_{k}\lambda^{\prime}_{k}|k^{\prime}\rangle\langle k^{\prime}|, (202)

and for the density matrices ϱk\varrho_{k}

ϱ=∑kλk′​ϱk\varrho=\sum_{k}\lambda^{\prime}_{k}\varrho_{k} (203)

holds. A minimization over 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} or 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} will lead to a larger value than a minimization over separable couplings. An optimization over 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} or 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} can efficiently be carried out using semidefinite programming for any system size. We can also consider the set of states that are classical-classical, which are the members of both 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} and 𝒞2.\mathcal{C}_{2}.

Let us consider now the case of the GMPC self-distance, when ϱ=σ.\varrho=\sigma. Then, a relevant coupling which is the elements of 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} and 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} is

ϱc​c=∑kλk​|k⟩​⟨k|⊗|k⟩​⟨k|,\varrho_{cc}=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}|k\rangle\langle k|\otimes|k\rangle\langle k|, (204)

where the eigendecomosition of ϱ\varrho is given in Eq. (9). For the coupling in Eq. (204), for N=1N=1 the equals

∑kλk​(Δ​H1)|k⟩2≤(Δ​H1)ϱ2.\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}(\Delta H_{1})^{2}_{|k\rangle}\leq(\Delta H_{1})^{2}_{\varrho}. (205)

So far, we have been obtaining results for the GMPC distance. Analogous statements hold for the DPT distance.

Another relevant case is the product state coupling

ϱ12=ϱ⊗σ.\varrho_{12}=\varrho\otimes\sigma. (206)

Then, we can define the distances given in Eqs. (5) and (1) for product states as

DGMPC,prod​(ϱ,σ)2=DDPT,prod​(ϱ,σ)2\displaystyle D_{\rm GMPC,prod}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}=D_{\rm DPT,prod}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}
=12​∑n=1NTr⁡[(Hn⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Hn)2​ϱ⊗σ]\displaystyle\quad=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N}{\rm Tr}[(H_{n}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes H_{n})^{2}\varrho\otimes\sigma]
=12​∑n=1N[(Δ​Hn)ϱ2+(Δ​Hn)σ2+(⟨Hn⟩ϱ−⟨Hn⟩σ)2],\displaystyle\quad=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left[(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\varrho}+(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\sigma}+(\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\varrho}-\langle{H_{n}}\rangle_{\sigma})^{2}\right],

c. f. Eq. (110). For the self-distance, the relation

DGMPC,prod​(ϱ,ϱ)=DDPT,prod​(ϱ,ϱ)=∑n=1N(Δ​Hn)ϱ2D_{\rm GMPC,prod}(\varrho,\varrho)=D_{\rm DPT,prod}(\varrho,\varrho)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\Delta H_{n})^{2}_{\varrho} (208)

holds.

In Table 1, we summarized the self-distances obtained for the Wasserstein distance considering an optimization over various subsets of the bipartite quantum states and N=1.N=1. For the quantities in the Table, the inequality given in Eq. (10) holds. As expected, a minimization over a larger set will not lead to a larger value and often will lead to a smaller value.

We can consider an optimization over other convex sets of states. For instance, a convex set can be characterzied by constraints like

(Δ​Ak)2≥ck(\Delta A_{k})^{2}\geq c_{k} (209)

or by the linear constraints

⟨Bk⟩≥dk,\langle{B_{k}}\rangle\geq d_{k}, (210)

where AkA_{k} and BkB_{k} are operators, ckc_{k} and dkd_{k} are constants. Other possibilities are the convex set of states with negativity not larger than a given bound [86], and the convex set of states not violating certain entanglement conditions. These conditions can be incorporated into the numerical optimization. We can also consider the convex set of states with a local hidden variable model [55, 56, 57].

10 Alternative definition of the Wasserstein distance such that the self-distance equals various generalized quantum Fisher information quantities

In this section, we will modify the definition of the Wasserstein distance such that the self-distance equals a quantity different from the ones we considered so far. In particular, we would like that it equals various generalized quantum Fisher information quantities. The Wigner-Yanase skew information and the quantum Fisher information are two members of this family.

The basic idea of Refs. [111, 112] is that for each standard matrix monotone function f:ℝ+→ℝ+,f:\mathbb{R}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+}, a generalized variance and a corresponding quantum Fisher information are defined. The notion standard means that ff must satisfy

f⁡(1)\displaystyle f(1) =1,\displaystyle=1, (211a)
f⁡(t)\displaystyle f(t) =t​f​(t−1).\displaystyle=tf(t^{-1}). (211b)

For a review on generalized variances, generalized quantum Fisher information quantities and covariances see Ref. [113]. Moreover, it is also useful to define the mean based on ff as

mf​(a,b)=a​f​(ba)m_{f}(a,b)=af\left(\frac{b}{a}\right) (212)

and use it instead of f.f. The normalization condition given in Eq. (211a) corresponds to the condition

mf​(a,a)=am_{f}(a,a)=a (213)

for the means. The requirement given in Eq. (211b) corresponds to

mf​(a,b)=mf​(b,a).m_{f}(a,b)=m_{f}(b,a). (214)

A list of generalized quantum Fisher information quantities generated by various well-known means mf​(a,b)m_{f}(a,b) can be found in Refs. [111, 112].

Using the normalization suggested by Ref. [62], we arrive at a family of generalized quantum Fisher information quantities FQf​[ϱ,H]F^{f}_{Q}[\varrho,H] such that (i) for pure states, we have

ℱQf​[|Ψ⟩,H]=4​(Δ​H)Ψ2.\mathcal{F}^{f}_{Q}[|\Psi\rangle,H]=4(\Delta H)^{2}_{\Psi}. (215)

(ii) For mixed states, FQf​[ϱ,H]F^{f}_{Q}[\varrho,H] is convex in the state.

The generalized variance varϱf​(H){\rm var}^{f}_{\varrho}(H) fulfills the following two requirements. (i) For pure states, the generalized variance equals the usual variance

varΨf​(H)=(Δ​H)Ψ2.{\rm var}^{f}_{\Psi}(H)=(\Delta H)^{2}_{\Psi}. (216)

(ii) For mixed states, varϱf​(H){\rm var}^{f}_{\varrho}(H) is concave in the state.

A family of generalized quantum Fisher information and generalized variance fulfilling the above requirements are [62]

ℱQf​[ϱ,H]\displaystyle{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}^{f}[\varrho,H] =2​∑k,lmf​(1,0)mf​(λk,λl)​(λk−λl)2​|Hk​l|2,\displaystyle=2\sum_{k,l}\frac{m_{f}(1,0)}{m_{f}(\lambda_{k},\lambda_{l})}{(\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{l})^{2}}|H_{kl}|^{2}, (217a)
varϱf​(H)\displaystyle{\rm var}_{\varrho}^{f}(H) =12​∑k,lmf​(λk,λl)mf​(1,0)​|Hk​l|2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k,l}\frac{m_{f}(\lambda_{k},\lambda_{l})}{m_{f}(1,0)}|H_{kl}|^{2}
−12​mf​(1,0)​|∑λk​Hk​k|2,\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2m_{f}(1,0)}\left|\sum\lambda_{k}H_{kk}\right|^{2}, (217b)

where the matrix elements of HH in the eigenbasis of ϱ\varrho are denoted as

Hk​l=⟨k|H|l⟩.H_{kl}=\langle k|H|l\rangle. (218)

ℱQf​[ϱ,H]/4{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}^{f}[\varrho,H]/4 has been called metric-adjusted skew information [114].

Note that the definition of the variance in Eq. (217b) requires that mf​(1,0)≡f⁡(0)m_{f}(1,0)\equiv f(0) is nonzero. In such cases ff is called regular [115].

The usual quantum Fisher information and the usual variance corresponds to

fmax​(x)=1+x2,f_{\max}(x)=\frac{1+x}{2}, (219)

and the arithmetic mean

mfmax​(a,b)=a+b2.m_{f_{\max}}(a,b)=\frac{a+b}{2}. (220)

Note that fmax​(x)f_{\max}(x) is the largest among standard matrix monotone functions. Due to this, ℱQfmax​[ϱ,H]{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}^{f_{\max}}[\varrho,H] is the largest among ℱQf​[ϱ,H]{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}^{f}[\varrho,H] and varϱfmax​(H){\rm var}_{\varrho}^{f_{\max}}(H) is the smallest among varϱf​(H).{\rm var}_{\varrho}^{f}(H).

The Wigner-Yanase skew information corresponds to

fWY​(x)=(x+1)24,f_{\rm WY}(x)=\frac{(\sqrt{x}+1)^{2}}{4}, (221)

and the mean

mfWY​(a,b)=(a+b)24.m_{f_{\rm WY}}(a,b)=\frac{(\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b})^{2}}{4}. (222)

Note that we get 4 times the usual Wigner-Yanase skew information due to the chosen normalization

ℱQfWY​[ϱ,H]=4​Iϱ​(H).\mathcal{F}^{f_{\rm WY}}_{Q}[\varrho,H]=4I_{\varrho}(H). (223)

We now show a method to express the various generalized quantum Fisher information quantities with each other.

(Xf)k​l=⟨k|X|l⟩=mf​(1,0)mf​(λk,λl).(X_{f})_{kl}=\langle k|X|l\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{m_{f}(1,0)}{m_{f}(\lambda_{k},\lambda_{l})}}. (224)

ℱQf1​[ϱ,H]=ℱQf2​[ϱ,Qf1,f2∘H],{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}^{f_{1}}[\varrho,H]={\mathcal{F}}^{f_{2}}_{Q}[\varrho,Q_{f_{1},f_{2}}\circ H], (225)

Next, we compute the matrix needed for f1=fWYf_{1}=f_{\rm WY} and f2=fmax.f_{2}=f_{\max}. We obtain, in the basis of the eigenvectors of ϱ,\varrho,

DGMPC,sepf​(ϱ,σ)2\displaystyle D^{f}_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}
=12​minϱ12\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\min_{\varrho_{12}}\; Tr⁡[(Yf∘H⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Yf∘H)2​ϱ12],\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[(Y_{f}\circ H\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes Y_{f}\circ H)^{2}\varrho_{12}],
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒮,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{S},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱ,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho,
Tr1​(ϱ12)=σ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\sigma. (239)

Based on Observation 10, for the self-distance

DGMPC,sepf​(ϱ,ϱ)2=14​ℱQf​[ϱ,H]D^{f}_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\varrho)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}^{f}[\varrho,H] (240)

holds.

Definition 9. A family of Wasserstein distance measures can be defined based on an optimization over general quantum states as

DDPTf​(ϱ,σ)2\displaystyle D^{f}_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2}
=12​minϱ12\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\min_{\varrho_{12}}\; Tr⁡{[(Zf∘H)T⊗𝟙−𝟙⊗Zf∘H]2​ϱ12},\displaystyle{\rm Tr}\{[(Z_{f}\circ H)^{T}\otimes\mathbbm{1}-\mathbbm{1}\otimes Z_{f}\circ H]^{2}\varrho_{12}\},
s. t. ϱ12∈𝒟,\displaystyle\varrho_{12}\in\mathcal{D},
Tr2​(ϱ12)=ϱT,\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{2}(\varrho_{12})=\varrho^{T},
Tr1​(ϱ12)=σ.\displaystyle{\rm Tr}_{1}(\varrho_{12})=\sigma. (241)

Based on Observation 10, for the self-distance

DDPTf​(ϱ,ϱ)2=14​ℱQf​[ϱ,H]D^{f}_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\varrho)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}{\mathcal{F}}_{Q}^{f}[\varrho,H] (242)

holds. It would be interesting to examine the properties of the quantities defined in Definitions 10 and 10.

11 Conclusions

We discussed how to define the quantum Wasserstein distance as an optimization over bipartite separable states rather than an optimization over general quantum states. With such a definition, the self-distance becomes related to the quantum Fisher information. We introduced also variance-like quantities in which we replaced the minimization used in the definition of the quantum Wasserstein distance by a maximization, and examined their properties. We discussed the relation of our findings to entanglement criteria. We examined also the quantity obtained after we considered optimizing the variance rather than the second moment in the usual expression of the quantum Wasserstein distance. Finally, we extended our results to the various generalized quantum Fisher information quantities. The details of the numerical calculations are discussed in Appendix A.

Appendix A Details of the numerical calculations

We used MATLAB [116] for numerical calculations. We used the semidefinite solver MOSEK [117] and the front-end YALMIP [118]. We also used the QUBIT4MATLAB package [119, 120]. DDPT​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm DPT}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} given in Definition 1 and DGMPC​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm GMPC}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} given in Definition 1 can be obtained using semidefinite programming. DGMPC,sep​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm GMPC,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} in Definition 5 and DDPT,sep​(ϱ,σ)2D_{\rm DPT,sep}(\varrho,\sigma)^{2} in Definition 5 need an optimization over separable states. The optimization over separable states can be carried out numerically using semidefinite programming for two qubits, since in this case the set of PPT states equals the set of separable states.

We included the routines computing the various quantum Wasserstein distance measures as wdistsquare_GMPC_ppt.m, wdistsquare_GMPC.m, wdistsquare_DPT_ppt.m, and wdistsquare_DPT.m. We included the various types of the variance-like quantities as wvar_GMPC_ppt.m, wvar_GMPC.m, wvar_DPT_ppt.m, and wvar_DPT.m. The usage of these routines is demonstrated in example_wdistsquare.m.
